subject: English
passage:
Text 1
Marine organisms are found throughout the world's oceans, even in challenging environments. They adapt to extreme pressures and temperatures. That's why Dr. Gifty Amponsah and her research team were surprised when water samples they collected from the deepest trenches of the Mariana Trench appeared to contain no detectable marine life. The finding doesn't definitively prove that no organisms exist at those depths, but the team says it does suggest that the extreme conditions severely limit organisms' ability to survive.

Text 2
Marine life exists in virtually every ocean environment on Earth. So it's improbable they would be entirely absent from Amponsah's team's sampling location, regardless of how extreme the deep-sea conditions are. There were likely so few organisms in the samples that existing detection methods couldn't identify them. But since a comparable volume of typical ocean water might contain thousands of organisms, the presence of so few in the deep trench samples would demonstrate how prohibitive the conditions are.
prompt: Based on the texts, Amponsah's team and the author of Text 2 would most likely agree with which statement about marine organisms?

choices.A: Most marine organisms are better adapted to survive in environments with extreme pressure than in environments with extreme temperatures.
choices.B: Most marine organisms are probably unable to withstand the conditions at the Mariana Trench study site.
choices.C: A much larger number of organisms would probably be found if another sample of water were taken from the Mariana Trench study site.
choices.D: Marine organisms are likely difficult to detect in the deep trench samples because they tend to be more transparent than organisms found in typical ocean water.

explanation:
Choice B is the best answer because it presents a statement about marine organisms with which Amponsah's team (Text 1) and the author of Text 2 would most likely agree. Text 1 states that marine organisms usually adapt to extreme pressures and temperatures, and so Amponsah's team was surprised when samples collected from the deepest trenches of the Mariana Trench appeared to contain no detectable marine life. Amponsah's team says that though this doesn't definitively prove no organisms exist at those depths, it suggests that organisms would have a notably difficult time surviving in the environment. The author of Text 2 says it's improbable that there would be no marine life at all in the deep-sea study site from which Amponsah's team retrieved water samples and that there may have been hard-to-detect organisms in the samples. However, the presence of only a few organisms in the deep trench samples rather than the thousands found in a typical ocean water sample (which would presumably be much easier to detect) would illustrate conditions in the deep trenches that make it difficult for organisms to thrive. Since Amponsah's team says that the apparent absence of organisms in the deep trench samples suggests an unusually harsh environment and the author of Text 2 says that even if there are a few undetectable organisms in the samples, the relatively tiny number of organisms would also suggest an unusually harsh environment, then Amponsah's team and the author of Text 2 would most likely agree that most marine organisms are unable to withstand the conditions at the Mariana Trench study site.

Why D is incorrect:

Choice D is incorrect. The author of Text 2 does speculate that there may have been so few organisms in the deep trench samples that existing detection methods couldn't identify them, but the author doesn't speculate that this is due to the transparency of the organisms. Moreover, nothing that Amponsah's team says suggests that they are speculating that their samples might have organisms that are more transparent than organisms in typical ocean water samples.
